**Contribution ID: repair-source-1**

**The failure began in the brief.** It converted an early homebuying dilemma into a specific shopping scene, then asked the writer to make that scene conversational. The source never establishes a finished condo, a renovated kitchen, two active listings, photos, a showing, or a buyer picturing furniture. Those details became most of A/B’s opening.

The real person is planning approximately ten months ahead. They are trying to work out what kind of ownership would improve their life. This is a stronger starting point than someone needing reassurance about liking a condo.

The complete source supplies these connected facts:

- The prospective buyer expects their budget could buy a “pretty decent condo” or an “okay house” likely needing work.
- They dislike the uncertainty of apartment “wall-mates.”
- Their current downstairs neighbors have fought noisily for four years; another neighbor plays weekend bass-heavy music.
- Their wonderfully ordinary preference is watching movies quietly.
- They consider their current Sherman Oaks rental excellent value.
- Their follow-up questions concern practical living: networking, power, layout, upkeep and older homes’ character. These are supporting context, not ingredients to cram into the post. [Original Reddit thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/SFV/comments/1tq96p1/looking_for_home_buying_advice_and_a_realtor_in/)

**The source’s strongest human tension:** a major first-home decision carries an almost embarrassingly modest hope—being able to enjoy an ordinary evening at home. The buyer fears trading one recurring problem for another.

That framing is an interpretation of the account, not a verified claim about why this person has decided to buy. The commenter’s belief that a detached home would solve the noise is also their belief, not an established property fact.

**Recommended fresh brief**

Create one post for the prospective buyer whose current neighbors have made quiet feel like an unusually important requirement for their first home. Center the modest daily experience they hope ownership will change. Let the hook establish homebuying and one recognizable unresolved tension immediately; the caption should make the reader understand why this seemingly small requirement has become such a big part of the search.

Use one complete on-screen hook. It should invite the reader into the situation without announcing Jen’s moral, explaining the property tradeoff, or supplying the emotional conclusion. The caption then develops the everyday frustration and gives Jen a natural role in the conversation: understanding what the buyer wants their next home to change and taking that seriously while the actual possibilities remain open.

Write as a believable, present-tense conversation with a prospective buyer. Do not present the source as Jen’s client or recreate its exact biography. The property-type dilemma can remain background; include it only if it advances the conversation. It is not the compulsory subject.

**Preservation decisions**

- Preserve the approved caption’s *movement*: it keeps discovering recognizable little moments—understanding on the phone, forgetting afterward, explaining to someone else, sending “???,” needing dinner. Each paragraph earns its place by making the relationship more believable.
- Preserve Jen’s directness, permission, varied rhythm and lightly amused recognition. Lowercase, an emoji and an empathetic sentence alone do not reproduce that craft.
- Preserve the complete reference as the structural benchmark and the approved Jen specimen as the voice authority. Kallaway’s original source explicitly favors an already established voice over blending creators.
- Adapt the hook architecture. The approved specimen resolves its on-screen exchange; Farrice’s new instruction explicitly calls for an unresolved hook answered in the caption. Copying the former beat pattern now would repeat the defect.

**Avoidance decisions**

Do not repair this by stripping the beat labels from A/B. Their underlying story still depends on invented property details, and their captions repeatedly explain a conclusion the screen has already delivered.

Do not overcorrect into vague suspense. A cold viewer must know they are entering a homebuying situation and recognize the concern before opening the caption. The missing information should be the story’s meaning or Jen’s response—not what the words refer to.

All reading and verification were read-only. No post drafted, files changed, or additional agents used.

Contribution ID: repair-craft-1
Status: FIRST DRAFT LOCKED before reading any editor diagnosis or feedback. All 769 lines of the frozen packet were read. The full repair-source-1 body was received through the conductor’s packet; no separate source-worker exchange is claimed.

On-screen text

“is it ridiculous that quiet neighbors are this high on my first-home wish list?”

Caption

how much of your neighbors’ business can you hear from your couch? 😂

because wanting to finish a movie without an argument coming through the floor doesn’t sound like a wild request to me.

and i get why you’d wonder whether buying a place would actually change that, or just give you new people to listen to.

tell me that when we talk about what you’re looking for. you don’t need to wait until you’ve decided between a house and a condo, or have a whole list ready.

i’m going to ask about the budget and bedrooms, of course. but if a quiet movie night is the thing you keep coming back to, i want that in the conversation too.

Private rationale

Accepted repair-source-1’s main correction: early uncertainty and the ordinary evening carry the post; no shopping scene or Jen client anecdote is invented. The hook locates a first-home buyer’s specific self-doubt and leaves Jen’s response for the caption. The caption moves from lightly amused recognition to the movie detail, then the risk of repeating the problem, then an invitation to explain that need before the buyer knows what to buy. This transfers the approved specimen’s conversational relationship and growing recognition without copying its resolved overlay exchange or sentence skeleton. The condo/house line only locates the buyer’s unresolved stage. No property type is offered as a noise solution. Gate A satisfied from the frozen packet; separate Gate B verification remains with the conductor/editor.

Contribution ID: repair-editor-1

Recommendation: revise before returning it. This is much clearer and more conversational than the failure described in the brief, but the hook puts the story on a feeling the source did not establish. My proposed changes preserve your voice and most of your opening. I have not read the solo route.

FULL INDEPENDENT PREFLIGHT POSITIONS, RETAINED FOR THIS REVIEW

The intended experience is recognition that becomes a better conversation with Jen. A cold viewer should immediately understand that someone is thinking about buying a home and that an ordinary part of living there complicates the decision. The hook needs a specific unanswered human question. The caption earns attention by making the concern more understandable, then showing what Jen would do with it. Curiosity cannot depend on unclear pronouns or withholding the subject.

The strongest material is the size mismatch: a huge purchase can carry a small-sounding hope for an ordinary evening. Stating that entire insight on screen and paraphrasing it below would exhaust the story before it starts. The first caption line must be the next natural thing Jen would say, not a second introduction or an explanation of the screen. One concrete recurring frustration should open the situation; later paragraphs must reveal something new about the buyer’s decision or Jen’s response. The finish should change what the reader can tell or ask Jen, or how Jen will help them think. A slogan about home, peace or deserving better would not earn the ending.

The approved specimen succeeds through accumulating recognition, not its beat count: understanding on the phone, getting confused later, explaining it to someone, sending a screenshot, still needing dinner. These are distinct turns in one conversation. Jen is funny because she recognizes actual behavior, and she takes responsibility for being understood. Here, her personality should come from a specific, lightly amused response and practical generosity. Lowercase plus an emoji cannot supply that relationship. We should not transfer the specimen’s permission structure by inventing an apology or insecurity for this buyer.

The source is an early planning account, approximately ten months ahead. Affordability, noise, movies, good rental value, upkeep questions and property preferences are self-reported. There is no inspected property, showing, finished kitchen, purchase outcome or Jen-client encounter. The author’s belief that a detached home would fix the noise is not ours to guarantee. The modest-evening interpretation is supported; shame, embarrassment, a sole buying motive or a settled priority are not established. A present-tense conversation can use the recognizable concern without narrating this stranger as Jen’s client or recreating their exact biography.

The likely failures remain turning the source into a condo-versus-house lesson, telling buyers merely that quiet matters, overpainting an invented evening, stacking more noise examples, or explaining the same emotional conclusion repeatedly. The opposite failure is compression into generic reassurance. Enough concrete progression must remain to earn Jen’s final contribution. Public output stays one On-screen text hook and Caption, with no beat apparatus or compulsory CTA.

WHAT THE ACTUAL DRAFT CHANGES IN MY ASSESSMENT

Your couch question is the best voice moment. It sounds like a person asking another person a knowing question, and the argument/movie line makes the concern concrete immediately. I would preserve both. The current hook, however, makes the reader ask whether quiet is a ridiculous priority. That is an invented self-doubt, not the source’s uncertainty. The source’s uncertainty is whether buying would improve daily life without creating another problem. Your third caption paragraph already contains that stronger story.

Your final two paragraphs also perform almost the same action: tell me about the quiet requirement / I want the quiet requirement in the conversation. They need a little more movement, not additional scenic writing. Make the first establish what Jen wants to understand; make the last take responsibility for helping before the buyer has settled the house-or-condo question.

I recommend moving the actual unresolved worry into the hook, replacing the now-redundant third paragraph with the source’s good-rent complication, and tightening the last two paragraphs into those distinct relational functions. Good rent is useful here because it explains why this is a real decision rather than an obvious instruction to move. It is one new fact, not another painted scene.

EXACT PROPOSED REVISION

On-screen text

“what if i buy my first home and the neighbors are just as loud?”

Caption

how much of your neighbors’ business can you hear from your couch? 😂

because wanting to finish a movie without an argument coming through the floor doesn’t sound like a wild request to me.

and when your rent is actually a good deal, i get why this isn’t a simple “just move” decision.

tell me that when we talk about what you’re looking for. i’ll ask about the budget and bedrooms, but i also want to know what you’re hoping will be different when you get home.

you don’t have to decide between a house and a condo before we talk. we can work through that part together.

WHY THIS WHOLE READING EFFECT

The hook now supplies buying context and an unresolved, source-grounded worry without answering it. The first caption question functions as Jen’s natural follow-up to that worry; it invites the everyday story instead of introducing a new subject. The movie then makes the concern specific. Good rent adds a distinct complication and helps the reader understand the decision. Jen’s contribution progresses from understanding the actual desired change to helping work through the still-open choice. The ending promises a conversation and help with the decision, not quieter neighbors.

The remaining permission-flavored phrase, “doesn’t sound like a wild request,” is secondary warmth inside Jen’s response. I would keep it because it is your natural voice line; it no longer requires the hook to claim the buyer felt ridiculous. The proposed question is an illustrative buyer concern, not a quotation attributed to the Reddit author or a claimed client encounter. No house or condo is presented as a noise guarantee.

This is my one complete advisory editorial contribution, not human approval or proof that the post will perform. You retain craft ownership and can accept or reject changes with reasons. No files changed, additional research performed, or other route inspected.
